The Uno has several GND pins, so the power-header GND wire is assigned GND.1 and the digital-header GND wire (next to AREF) is assigned GND.3.

The tutorial's main example is two UNO boards with 'old style' wiring: programmer D11/D12/D13 to target D11/D12/D13 (MOSI/MISO/SCK), programmer D10 to target RESET, 5V to 5V, GND to GND. I modelled this rather than the ICSP-header variant.
The ICSP header is not a port on the arduino-uno catalogue entry, so the D11-D13 pins are used.

The 10uF capacitor between programmer RESET and GND is required when the programmer is a UNO. Positive leg goes to RESET. I put it on the breadboard (cols 1-2) and added the programmer RESET and GND wires to the breadboard. The text says to place it after the ArduinoISP sketch is uploaded.

The three optional status LEDs follow the ArduinoISP sketch pins: heartbeat on D9, error on D8, programming on D7. The manual's LED image was not available, so the breadboard layout and the 220 ohm series resistors are assumptions. Each resistor goes from the LED cathode to the ground rail.
Both boards are powered and programmed over USB from the computer (not modelled). The manual says not to connect USB or power while wiring.

The LED on channel n is led n (W n); the code addresses channels 0-5, with addresses 000 for W1 through 101 for W6 per the datasheet.

Pi-stop is a new part type; its ports are modelled as header-sockets and R/A/G each conduct through an LED to the common GND.
The Pi's power, USB and software (Mu, gpiozero) are not modelled as parts.

Breadboard orientation: the image labels its upper half j-f and lower half e-a, so the upper half is catalogue bank 'b' (rows f-j) and the lower half is bank 't' (rows a-e). The rail drawn along the bottom of the breadboard (next to row a) is therefore catalogue rail 'tn'.
The sensor's four pins go into column 1-4 of row j (VCC, Trig, Echo, GND). Jumper wires leave from row f of the same columns.

The image colours column 4 (rows e-a) black, but the Echo (blue) wire ends in column 4 row d and the 330 ohm resistor starts at 4c. I treated this as the Echo node and not as ground, since it would otherwise short Echo to ground.

Potential divider: Echo -> 330 ohm (r1) -> junction at column 8 -> GPIO17 (blue wire) and junction -> 470 ohm (r2) -> column 12 -> black wire to the ground rail. The junction is column 8 bank t: r1 at 8t.c, wire at 8t.e, r2 at 8t.b. This is the same strip.

Pi pins: 5V is the first pin in the top header row (physical pin 2, named 5V.1). Trig goes to GPIO4 (pin 7). The divider output goes to GPIO17 (pin 11). Ground is the last pin in the bottom row (physical pin 39). I chose the port name GND.8 for it, because the catalogue treats all GND pins as interchangeable.
Ground rail wires are plugged into rail holes tn.12, tn.24 and tn.28. They are treated as one rail strip, as the catalogue defines.
No breadboard or separate jumper wires are used: the battery pack and motors have their own fixed leads, which are screwed into the controller board's terminal blocks.
Battery red lead goes to VIN and black lead to GND, as the manual requires. The battery pack is switched off while wiring.
Motors can go either way round, so the left motor is Motor B and the right motor is Motor A. The terminal labels in the photos are only partly legible, so the A/B assignment is inferred.

The board sits on the Pi's GPIO header, so the board's GPIO ports are header-sockets and the Pi's are header-pins. This fixes the incompatible header-pin to header-pin pairs. The manual says the board uses GPIO 7, 8, 9 and 10. Only those and one GND pin are modelled. Its other pass-through pins are ignored.
Which GPIO pin drives which motor terminal is not given, so no through-connections are modelled inside the controller board.
The header GND pin is taken as the Pi's GND.1. The exact GND pin is not shown.
The 4xAA battery pack is not in the catalogue, so it is a new type with POS and NEG leads and a built-in on/off switch.
Breadboard ravine separates top bank (t, rows a-e) from bottom bank (b, rows f-j). The manual's 'row 1' is taken as column 1 of the catalogue's naming.
LED anode (long leg) in 1t.e on the left/top side of the ravine; cathode in 1b.f on the other side. Wire1's male end goes in 1t.a, which is the same strip as the anode.
Resistor leg 1 shares the cathode strip (1b.h is in column 1 bottom bank). Leg 2 goes in column 5 bottom bank (any free row on that side); wire2 male end shares that strip (5b.j).
Resistor value is not given in the manual; 330 ohm assumed as typical for 3.3 V.
Jumper-wire-mf: port 'a' is assumed to be the male end (breadboard) and 'b' the female end (Pi header pin).
The Pi's 3V3 pin is 3V3.1 and GND is GND.1; the manual does not specify which physical pins, so these were chosen.

The Pi header is drawn with GND highlighted at the left-column pin (physical pin 9) and GP17 at physical pin 11. I used GND.1 for the GND pin because the exact GND index isn't shown; the GND pins are symmetric.

The black wire goes to breadboard hole 15a and the purple wire to 18a. The buzzer covers the right-hand holes and hides them, so I assumed its legs are in column e of rows 15 and 18, on the same strips as the wires.
The buzzer's polarity is not labelled. I assumed port 1 is the positive (longer) leg, at row 18 and GPIO17, and port 2 is the negative leg, at row 15 and GND.
No resistor is used. The manual says an active buzzer doesn't need one.
The manual text only covers the active buzzer, so the part is the catalogue 'buzzer' type.

This is a MakeCode block-programming project. The only hardware is a micro:bit using its built-in 5x5 LED display and on-board buttons A and B. The manual shows no wires, breadboard or external components.

Assumption: the manual says to write the program in the MakeCode editor and transfer the .hex file onto the micro:bit. That needs a USB cable, and the micro:bit needs power, so I added one USB cable (usb1) joined to the micro:bit's USB port. The manual does not show it, and its far end (computer or power) is left unmodelled.
The micro:bit is not in the catalogue, so I added a new part type 'microbit'. Its ports are the two on-board buttons and the USB connector.
The program logic (forever loop, random pause, while not A and not B pressed, if A/B shows an arrow) is software and is not modelled as graph edges.
The two images show the 'while not (A pressed) and not (B pressed)' block, in Arabic. They agree with the manual's text.

The wiring diagram is treated as the authority: the Pi header pins used are GPIO25 (orange wire, red LED), GPIO8 (green wire, amber LED), GPIO7 (pink wire, green LED), GPIO21 (purple wire, button) and GPIO15 (blue wire, buzzer). The manual text lists amber=28 and green=27, which do not match the diagram.
Resistor value is not stated in the manual; 330 ohm assumed.
The black wire from the Pi goes to the GND pin next to GP3 (physical pin 6); mapped to GND.1.

The right-hand breadboard rail that all grounds use is modelled as the 'tn' rail (one strip); hole numbers on it (tn.3, tn.6, tn.9, tn.15, tn.21, tn.28) are approximate, since they all sit on the same strip.
LED anodes are on the resistor side (column j, rows 9/15/21) and cathodes go to the ground rail; buzzer + (port 1) is on row 4 column j, its other leg to the ground rail.
Button: row 28 is side 1 (1.l/1.r) wired to the GND rail, row 30 is side 2 (2.l/2.r) wired to GPIO21; button straddles the centre gap (e and f columns). Button uses Pi internal pull-up in software.
The colour of the middle LED is yellow in the diagram but called 'amber' in the manual.
Breadboard orientation: the image's upper half (rows j-f) is treated as catalogue bank 'b' and the lower half (rows e-a) as bank 't'; resistors bridge the centre gap from column Nb.f to Nt.e.
Column numbers were estimated from the image: LEDs at columns 10/11, 13/14, 16/17, 19/20, 22/23; blue wires land on row d of columns 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.

LED anode is taken as the left leg (resistor side) and cathode as the right leg, matching the schematic. The five short black wires join each cathode column (row i) to the top negative rail; exact rail hole numbers (tn.12, 15, 18, 21, 24) are approximate, and all rail holes are one strip anyway.
The Uno GND pin next to AREF on the digital header is named GND.1; the catalogue does not say which GND index that is.
Signal pin mapping: 6->LED1, 5->LED2, 4->LED3, 3->LED4, 2->LED5, as in the schematic. The Uno is powered and read over USB for serial input; the USB cable is not drawn and is omitted.

The breadboard is drawn with rows f-j in the upper half and a-e in the lower half. In the catalogue's naming, bank 't' is rows a-e and bank 'b' is rows f-j. So the upper holes are written as '9b.i' and the lower holes as '6t.b'.
Rail hole numbers (tp.1, tn.2, tn.10, tn.25, bp.3, bn.5 and so on) are estimates from the picture. Each rail is one strip, so the exact number does not change the circuit.
The 5V wire goes to the top '+' rail. The ground wire goes to the top '-' rail, from the second GND pin on the power header, which I called GND.2.
A black wire joins the top '-' rail to the bottom '-' rail. A red wire joins the top '+' rail to the bottom '+' rail.
The speaker is not in the catalogue, so I added 'speaker-8ohm' as a new part type. Its red lead goes to the 100 ohm resistor at column 12. Its black lead goes to the ground rail.
The 100 ohm resistor sits between column 9 (pin 8 wire) and column 12 (speaker red lead).
Each FSR has one lead in the bottom '+' rail and one lead in a column (6, 16 or 24). That column also holds the 10k resistor to the bottom '-' rail and a yellow wire to an analog pin.
Analog pin mapping: A2 goes to column 6, A1 to column 16 and A0 to column 24. I traced the yellow wires in the circuit image and checked them against the schematic.
The picture shows each FSR with three drawn legs (two lines and a green shaded area). I modelled each as the catalogue 'fsr' with two ports.
The 10k resistor value is written as 10000 (ohms), following the catalogue's 'value=220' style.
